title: Garden Party

jokes.text: Andy excitedly asks about the billboard campaign, not yet knowing it's been defaced with phallic graffiti
jokes.setup: Andy enthusiastically pitches the billboard ad campaign as a smart business move featuring his own face
jokes.punchline: The colleague's barely-suppressed laughter reveals the billboard has been defaced — the dramatic irony of Andy's pride vs. reality
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom dramatic irony — the audience and colleague know something Andy doesn't. Works well as an opener but not particularly original. Andy's ego-forward delivery makes it character-specific.

jokes.text: Talking-head: 'There's this thing that people tend to do with billboards... if there's an opportunity for a graffiti artist to work in a phallic shape interacting with the artwork, it'll happen. And Andy gave them that opportunity.'
jokes.setup: Jim is asked to explain what happened to the billboard
jokes.punchline: The clinical, almost sociological framing of 'graffiti artists working in a phallic shape interacting with the artwork' — treating crude vandalism as an inevitable natural phenomenon
jokes.explanation: This is peak Jim Halpert confessional — the comedic voice is so specific to the character. The pseudo-anthropological framing ('if there's an opportunity... it'll happen') elevates a crude joke into something genuinely witty. 'And Andy gave them that opportunity' is a perfect button. The restraint is the joke, and it's brilliantly executed.

jokes.text: Andy's reaction upon learning the billboard says '20 dongs' — 'Great billboard. Funny, edgy, right up to the line without crossing it. Loved it.' when asked which one he saw
jokes.setup: Andy is desperately trying to save face about his defaced billboard
jokes.punchline: He pivots to claiming he intentionally loved the defaced version — 'right up to the line without crossing it' — which is delusional self-justification
jokes.explanation: Very Andy — the inability to admit embarrassment and the immediate pivot to 'I meant to do that' energy. 'Right up to the line without crossing it' applied to 20 penises on his face is a well-constructed piece of character comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight's dawning horror upon realizing the billboard featuring him and Andy has been defaced — 'No. No. No, no, no, no, no, no'
jokes.setup: Andy mentions the billboard was from the photo shoot with both of them
jokes.punchline: Dwight's repeated 'No' cascading into full existential panic — then a 30-second gap implying he's seen the image on a phone/screen and is spiraling
jokes.explanation: The extended 'No' repetition followed by ~30 seconds of implied visual reaction (seeing the defaced billboard) is classic mockumentary physical comedy. The rewatch bonus is high because you know exactly what's happening off-screen. The sustained silence at 01:29 is the actual punchline.

jokes.text: ~30 seconds of Dwight apparently looking at his phone/screen showing the defaced billboard — pure reaction, no dialogue
jokes.setup: Dwight has just realized the billboard featuring him has been covered in phallic graffiti
jokes.punchline: The extended silence/reaction shot — the audience imagines the image; Dwight's face does the rest
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is entirely visual and structural — the long silence IS the joke. The Office uses this device masterfully. The audience's imagination fills in the image. Strong rewatch value because you catch Dwight's specific expressions.

jokes.text: Dwight giving directions to Schrute Farms via soil acidity: 'If the soil starts to get acidic, you've probably gone too far.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is giving pre-party instructions including directions to the farm
jokes.punchline: His directions include tasting/testing soil acidity as a navigational landmark — perfectly Dwight, completely impractical
jokes.explanation: Pure Dwight. Only Dwight Schrute could give directions using soil pH. The specificity ('acidic') makes it feel like genuine Schrute logic rather than random absurdism. It's character-integrated absurdism at its best — the joke couldn't be told by any other character on any other show.

jokes.text: 'Just give us the address, we'll look it up online.' / 'It's simpler this way.' / 'It's really not.'
jokes.setup: Colleagues push back on Dwight's soil-acidity directions
jokes.punchline: Dwight's complete confidence that his absurd system is simpler than Google Maps
jokes.explanation: Good button on the directions joke. The straight-man 'it's really not' is perfectly delivered and economical. A solid supporting beat rather than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Darryl's response to Dwight's 'no burping, no slurping, chew thoroughly' lecture: 'What happens when we're done chewing? Do we spit it out on the floor or keep it in our mouths the rest of the time?'
jokes.setup: Dwight delivers an over-the-top lecture on table manners as if the office are feral children
jokes.punchline: Darryl weaponizes Dwight's condescension by asking a deliberately idiotic follow-up question — exposing the absurdity of the lecture
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. Darryl's dry wit is perfectly deployed here — by asking an obviously stupid question he exposes that Dwight IS treating them like children. The structure is excellent: Dwight sets up the absurd premise, Darryl pushes it to its logical extreme. The question is also genuinely funny as a standalone piece of absurdist logic. High quotability, strong Darryl character moment.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I promise to be under-bearing for a week if you guys just all step it up.'
jokes.setup: Andy admits he's being overbearing about party manners
jokes.punchline: 'Under-bearing' as if it's the opposite and equally valid management mode — Andy using malapropism-adjacent logic to negotiate
jokes.explanation: 'Under-bearing' is an Andy-specific bit of verbal construction. It works because it reveals his faulty negotiating logic — the word sounds reasonable but is meaningless. Mild laugh, good character texture.

jokes.text: 'This is not a picnic, Phyllis. It's a garden party. There are rules.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis innocuously calls the event a picnic
jokes.punchline: Andy's hair-trigger correction and the gravely serious 'There are rules' — treating the distinction as a matter of enormous importance
jokes.explanation: Solid Andy character beat. The specificity of 'There are rules' as a statement about garden parties is funny because of how seriously he means it. Consistent with the episode's theme of Andy's performative class anxiety.

jokes.text: Andy's description of 'Connecticut casual' dress code, and someone asking if it's 'Pennsylvania business, i.e., this is what I'm wearing to your party'
jokes.setup: Andy announces a dress code of 'Connecticut casual'
jokes.punchline: The colleague reframes it as 'Pennsylvania business' — essentially 'whatever I already have on' — deflating Andy's pretension with Scranton pragmatism
jokes.explanation: The class/geography juxtaposition of 'Connecticut casual' vs. 'Pennsylvania business' is sharp writing. It lands on a real cultural truth about Andy's Connecticut upbringing vs. Scranton reality, and the sardonic 'i.e., this is what I'm wearing' button is excellent. Punches above its weight.

jokes.text: Andy's family garden party video — 'Who's the sausage?' referring to Andy's brother in the viral video
jokes.setup: Andy proudly shows a video of his family's successful garden party
jokes.punchline: Kevin's obliviously rude 'Who's the sausage?' about Andy's brother — said with complete innocence
jokes.explanation: Peak Kevin — blurting out what everyone might be thinking with zero social filter. 'Sausage' is a funny enough insult word. The comedy is entirely in the delivery and character specificity. Lands well in the room.

jokes.text: Andy singing along to his family's video: 'It's my dad and my brother / I would have joined in but this melody doesn't really support another harmony part, so'
jokes.setup: Andy shows his family's viral garden party video featuring a father-son duet
jokes.punchline: Andy's transparent post-hoc rationalization for why he wasn't included — the elaborate musical excuse when the real answer is he wasn't invited to join
jokes.explanation: Excellent Andy moment. The specific musical excuse ('this melody doesn't really support another harmony part') is brilliantly in-character — it sounds like something only a music-obsessed person would say, but it's clearly a defense mechanism. Seeds the episode's emotional core (Andy's family rejection) while being genuinely funny. High character integration.

jokes.text: Andy's awkward cover story: 'Did Robert California get an invite? Yeah, of course. I mean, yeah. I think he did.'
jokes.setup: A colleague asks if Robert California was invited, clearly seeing through the party's real purpose
jokes.punchline: Andy's stumbling non-answer confirms what everyone suspects — the party is to impress Robert
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe beat. Andy's inability to conceal his motivations is a consistent character trait. Not especially original but serves the story well.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'Why didn't you just say this was to impress Robert California?'
jokes.setup: Andy has been performing elaborate party planning without stating his obvious motive
jokes.punchline: Jim cuts through all of it with one flat, exasperated question directly to camera
jokes.explanation: Classic Jim camera-talking-head function — articulating what the audience is thinking. Economical but not particularly inventive. The joke is more structural (mockumentary format) than written.

jokes.text: Gabe's talking head: 'Classic Gabe move. Hey, Andy, how about you don't steal my business strategies and I won't dress like my life is just one long brunch.'
jokes.setup: Gabe watches Andy throw a party to impress the CEO — exactly what Gabe would do
jokes.punchline: Gabe calling it a 'Classic Gabe move' then pivoting to a vicious comeback about Andy's preppy aesthetic — 'dress like my life is just one long brunch'
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Dress like my life is just one long brunch' is genuinely brilliant — it's precise, visual, character-specific, and devastating. The structure is perfect: Gabe admits Andy's move is exactly what he'd do, then pivots to the insult. It works on multiple levels: Gabe's self-awareness, his cattiness, and the accuracy of the burn. High quotability — this is the kind of line people remember and repeat. Comparable in quality to an 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Street view of Schrute Farms on Google Maps — the camera apparently caught something embarrassing on the farm
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam type the address into Google Maps and check street view
jokes.punchline: 'They don't warn you when the cameras are driving by' — implying something mortifying was captured on Google Street View at the farm
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely visual — what we see on the screen is the punchline, which isn't accessible in transcript form. The implication (something Dwight/Mose was doing got captured) is funny in concept. Strong rewatch value because the actual image is presumably worth seeing. Text alone undersells it.

jokes.text: Dwight reveals his 'secret weapon' for the party — a $2 book on garden party hosting — which turns out to be Jim's self-published fake book written to manipulate Dwight
jokes.setup: Dwight brags about a rare, one-of-a-kind garden party book he found online for $2
jokes.punchline: Cut to Jim's talking head revealing he wrote and self-published the book specifically to mess with Dwight — and he's disappointed it only sold one copy
jokes.explanation: The best structural joke in the episode, possibly one of the best Jim pranks in the entire series. The layering is exceptional: (1) Dwight's smugness about his 'secret weapon,' (2) the reveal that it's Jim's book, (3) Jim's disappointment that only ONE person bought it — which means Dwight was the sucker he was calling out. 'Some sucker on the Internet sold it to me for $2' is Dwight calling himself a sucker. The economy of the reveal, the long-game nature of the prank, and the bonus joke about poor book sales make this exceptional. Easily the episode's standout joke.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'I'm actually really disappointed in how poorly my book is doing. I've only sold one copy.'
jokes.setup: Jim reveals he's the author of Dwight's 'rare' garden party book
jokes.punchline: Jim's completely straight delivery of disappointment about book sales — as if the goal was literary success rather than one specific target
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the book reveal. Jim treating his one-sale prank book like a legitimate publishing disappointment is a brilliant extension of the joke. The deadpan is flawless — 'I've only sold one copy' lands because Jim seems genuinely, earnestly let down. It deepens an already great joke with additional absurdist logic. High quotability.

jokes.text: Angela pregnancy small-talk: cankles, cup size, the senator being 'grossed out'
jokes.setup: Casual pregnancy conversation in the office
jokes.punchline: Angela oversharing that the senator is 'grossed out' by her pregnancy changes — dark comedy about her cold marriage
jokes.explanation: The 'senator is grossed out' detail is the best beat here — it reveals the loveless nature of Angela's marriage in a quick throwaway. The cankles/cup size setup is functional but not particularly sharp. Works as character texture more than standalone comedy.

jokes.text: Philip name collision — both Pam's baby and Angela's baby are going to be named Philip, for entirely different reasons, revealed in escalating awkward beats
jokes.setup: Angela whispers that her baby's name will be Philip (after her favorite cat); Pam reveals her baby will also be Philip (after her grandfather)
jokes.punchline: Both women stake their claims, both names are ridiculous for opposite reasons (a cat vs. a dead grandfather promise), and neither will back down
jokes.explanation: The double Philip reveal is a solid bit. The contrast of justifications (cat vs. grandfather) is funny in itself. Angela's 'It's after my favorite cat' delivered with the same gravity as Pam's sentimental grandfather story is well-constructed. The competitive tension between the two women adds cringe.

jokes.text: 'Gretchen, I need another marmalade.'
jokes.setup: Andy agrees to the basil plant after the marmalade has apparently already been promised to Robert's sister
jokes.punchline: Robert has an assistant named Gretchen who sources his hostess gifts — a strangely powerful man detail applied to bringing jam to a party
jokes.explanation: The button on the marmalade scene. Four words, enormous implication — Robert California has dedicated staff managing his marmalade inventory. The economy is superb. It reframes Robert as operating on a completely different power level even in absurd contexts. High quotability precisely because of its brevity and the world it implies.

jokes.text: Mose as the valet — aggressively demanding guests surrender their cars, physically blocking them, refusing all reasonable alternatives
jokes.setup: Guests arrive at Schrute Farms and encounter Mose acting as valet
jokes.punchline: Mose's valet approach is essentially carjacking — the intensity and physicality of 'Get out of your car. Get out.' vs. the absurdity of valet parking at a farm
jokes.explanation: Mose as valet is a reliably funny recurring character deployment. The physical comedy of him forcing people out of cars at what is essentially a beet farm works well. The contrast of 'valet' formality with Mose's feral energy is the joke. Strong visual comedy that plays better on screen than on paper.

jokes.text: Mose: 'Have a good time at the thing. It's a little tricky. You might want to—'
jokes.setup: After forcing guests out of their cars, Mose offers what sounds like a helpful warning
jokes.punchline: The sentence trails off incompletely — Mose apparently drives away or wanders off mid-sentence, the warning forever unfinished
jokes.explanation: The incomplete trailing-off sentence is a perfectly Mose bit — he starts to communicate like a human and can't complete it. 'At the thing' is also funny. The joke is in the incompleteness. Works better on screen where you see the car disappearing.

jokes.text: Dwight announcing guests from Jim's fake garden party book: 'Chapter Two. Announcing guests as they enter is the height of decorum. The more volume displayed, the more honour is bestowed upon everyone present.'
jokes.setup: Dwight consults his 'rare' book to host the garden party properly
jokes.punchline: The book instructs him to announce guests at maximum volume — which Dwight follows with complete sincerity, humiliating everyone — all because Jim wrote absurd instructions specifically to make Dwight do this
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff of the Jim's-book long con, and it delivers magnificently. The book's pompous prose ('height of decorum,' 'honour is bestowed upon everyone present') is perfectly written fake Victorian nonsense. The genius is that Jim wrote something that SOUNDS plausibly like a real etiquette book. Dwight's total commitment to executing the absurd instruction while guests arrive is cringe perfection. One of the episode's structural highlights.

jokes.text: Dwight announces: 'Stanley Hudson and his mistress, Cynthia.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is announcing guests as instructed by the book, loudly, to bestow maximum honor
jokes.punchline: He announces Stanley's affair partner as 'his mistress Cynthia' in front of everyone — presumably including Stanley's wife if she's present — with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Probably the single funniest moment in the episode as delivered. The specificity of 'and his mistress, Cynthia' — Dwight knows enough to know she's a mistress and announces it at top volume — is shocking and hilarious. It works on multiple levels: the callback to Jim's book, the callback to Stanley's affair, and Dwight's absolute sincerity. The audience reaction would be enormous. Near-perfect economy — four words carry an enormous comedic payload. High quotability. Classic Office.

jokes.text: Dwight announces: 'James, Pamela, and Peepee Halpert.'
jokes.setup: Dwight continues loudly announcing guests with 'maximum volume for maximum honour'
jokes.punchline: He announces the Halperts' daughter Cece as 'Peepee Halpert' — either intentionally mocking or because Jim wrote that instruction into the book
jokes.explanation: Following 'Stanley Hudson and his mistress Cynthia,' this maintains the momentum perfectly. 'Peepee Halpert' is funny both as a childish insult and because it's possibly something Jim wrote into his own book, making him a victim of his own prank. The irony is rich. High quotability.

jokes.text: Andy to Mable: 'Mable, Mable, if you're able, keep your elbows off the table.'
jokes.setup: Andy is nervously hovering over guests, correcting their behavior
jokes.punchline: He recites a condescending children's etiquette rhyme to an adult guest — completely oblivious to how insulting this is
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe beat. Andy treating his colleagues like children at a finishing school is a consistent running thread of his character's class anxiety. The nursery rhyme is a nice touch of specificity. Not exceptional but functional.

jokes.text: Andy's parents arrive and immediately correct that Andy is not the CEO but merely the regional manager: 'I thought you were the CEO.' / 'I don't know how you got there. You said you were running the company.' / 'This branch. I'm the regional manager.' / 'That makes more sense.'
jokes.setup: Andy introduces his parents to Robert California
jokes.punchline: His parents have apparently been told Andy runs 'the company' — the correction in front of Robert ('that makes more sense') is devastatingly condescending
jokes.explanation: This scene efficiently establishes Andy's parental dynamic through pure cringe. 'That makes more sense' is the kill shot — delivered presumably with complete innocence by the father, but devastating in front of the actual CEO. The structure is excellent: setup (Andy's implied boasting), middle (correction), punchline (dismissive confirmation). Strong character work that pays off in the episode's emotional arc.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'Did I throw this party to impress my parents? That's crazy. No, if they wanted a garden party, they could throw one themselves. Which, as a matter of fact, they did last week. They threw one for my baby brother, and it was totally amazing. But I couldn't care less.'
jokes.setup: Andy is asked if he threw the party to impress his parents
jokes.punchline: His 'denial' collapses into a rambling admission — the baby brother party detail, 'totally amazing,' and 'but I couldn't care less' back-to-back is textbook unreliable narrator
jokes.explanation: Classic Office confessional structure — the character's denial immediately undercuts itself. 'But I couldn't care less' following 'it was totally amazing' is the type of obvious self-deception that The Office does brilliantly. Andy's talking heads are among the show's best because Ed Helms commits completely. Well-structured descent from denial to inadvertent admission.

jokes.text: Andy's parents have theatre tickets — to see 'Moneyball' — 'It was Walter Jr.'s choice.'
jokes.setup: Andy's parents announce they can't stay long because they have theatre tickets
jokes.punchline: 'Moneyball' — a baseball movie — is what they're calling 'theatre,' and it's Walter Jr.'s choice, not something Andy selected, implying Andy's brother controls the evening's entertainment
jokes.explanation: A quiet little joke — 'Moneyball' as 'theatre' is funny, and 'Walter Jr.'s choice' twists the knife slightly on Andy's sibling rivalry. Understated but effective. The Bernards calling a movie 'theatre' suggests they consider any outing with their preferred son a cultural event.

jokes.text: Walter Jr. introduces himself to Jim: 'Tuna, right?' — using Jim's office nickname — and Jim's visible surprise that the brother knows his nickname
jokes.setup: Walter Jr. meets Jim Halpert for the first time
jokes.punchline: 'Tuna, right?' — Walter Jr. knows Andy's nickname for Jim, revealing Andy talks about his work friends to his family, which is somehow simultaneously endearing and slightly pathetic given the family dynamic
jokes.explanation: An economical character beat. 'Tuna, right?' does a lot of work — it reveals Andy's family life, the depth of his attachment to his work friends, and subtly makes him more sympathetic. Jim's implied double-take is the visual comedy. Good economy.

jokes.text: Walter Jr. to Pam: 'No. Hell no. She wishes. No, no, no, no, no. No.' — about whether Pam is with him
jokes.setup: Jim introduces Pam as his wife
jokes.punchline: Walter Jr.'s escalating, enthusiastic refusal — 'Hell no. She wishes.' — is so aggressive about NOT being with Pam that it's both an insult to Pam and a strange display for someone who just met Jim
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the overkill of the denial — 'She wishes' implies he thinks Pam is attracted to him after two seconds. It's good for establishing Walter Jr. as insufferably confident, setting up his dynamic with Andy. Not a standout gag but functionally effective.

jokes.text: Dwight reading from Jim's book: 'Chapter Four. One of the host's most important duties is as dance master. A proper courtly dance sets the tone for the entire afternoon.' — then apparently attempting to lead a courtly dance
jokes.setup: Dwight continues following Jim's ridiculous garden party book instructions
jokes.punchline: Dwight attempts to 'set the tone' with a formal courtly dance — which would be mortifying for everyone present and completely sincere from Dwight
jokes.explanation: The dance master instruction is another great deployment of Jim's book — the fake Victorian prose is consistently well-written, and Dwight's execution would be visually hilarious. This beat works as an escalation of the book prank.

jokes.text: Robert California's grand entrance — announced by Dwight at maximum volume — 'Ladies and gentlemen, may I present... Robert California.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been following the book's instruction to announce guests loudly; Robert California arrives
jokes.punchline: Robert California — the CEO, the most powerful and unsettling person in the room — gets the full theatrical announcement treatment from Dwight, and Robert presumably emerges having been announced like a medieval lord
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the guest announcement gag — if 'Stanley Hudson and his mistress' was the peak shock announcement, Robert California getting the full herald treatment is the absurdist peak. Robert's reaction (or lack thereof) would be the visual punchline.

jokes.text: Kevin is apparently suspended or elevated in some contraption at the party: 'This is not funny, man. Let me down. I think this thing is broken.' / 'It's not broken, Kevin. This is how it works.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has apparently gotten into or been placed in some garden party apparatus Dwight set up
jokes.punchline: Dwight's complete certainty that the thing is working correctly vs. Kevin being trapped/elevated against his will
jokes.explanation: Revisiting Kevin's predicament for a second beat. Dwight's 'This is how it works' delivered with absolute authority about a mechanism that has trapped a large man is consistently funny. The visual of Kevin suspended somewhere at a garden party is inherently comic.

jokes.text: Andy's toast strategy: 'Toasts are great. I mean, you toast somebody, they toast you back. It just goes round and round. That's my favourite part about toasts, the reciprocity.'
jokes.setup: Andy initiates the toast sequence, clearly trying to engineer a toast to Robert California
jokes.punchline: His transparent explanation of the 'reciprocity' system — he wants Robert to feel obligated to toast him back, stated baldly as if it's a universal truth about toasting
jokes.explanation: Andy's toast manipulation plan is character-specific and mildly insightful about sycophantic management behavior. The 'reciprocity' speech is delivered with enough earnestness to be funny — he actually believes this is a legitimate strategy. Good setup for the toast sequence to follow.

jokes.text: Someone toasts Robert California. Kelly immediately yells 'Yay, Robert!'
jokes.setup: A colleague makes a toast to Robert California
jokes.punchline: Kelly's enthusiastic 'Yay, Robert!' — performative cheerfulness that suggests she doesn't know or care about Robert but reflexively cheers anything social
jokes.explanation: Two words, perfect Kelly. Her reflexive enthusiasm is character-perfect. Brief but lands as a quick laugh.

jokes.text: Gabe's talking head: 'I cannot believe I didn't think of toasting Robert. Get in the game, Gabriel.'
jokes.setup: Oscar and Kelly toast Robert California before Gabe can
jokes.punchline: Gabe is angry at himself for missing the sycophantic opportunity — 'Get in the game, Gabriel' — talking to himself like a sports coach about ass-kissing
jokes.explanation: Gabe self-coaching in a sports metaphor about the most pathetic possible competitive arena is very funny. 'Get in the game, Gabriel' using his full name adds a layer — like a disappointed parent. High character integration, good economy. Gabe's self-awareness about his own brownnosing while still doing it is sharp writing.

jokes.text: Gabe to Andy: 'Why are you talking to Stanley's mistress?' — whispering at the party
jokes.setup: The party continues; Andy mingles
jokes.punchline: Gabe casually references 'Stanley's mistress' as if this is now common knowledge — callback to Dwight's earlier announcement outing the affair
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Dwight's announcement — it confirms that the outing was real and is now common knowledge at the party. The casual way Gabe says it, as if it's just a fact about Stanley, is the joke. Economical callback.

jokes.text: Ryan toasts 'someone who isn't here but who will be in just four short months — Welcome to the world, Philip Lipton.'
jokes.setup: The toast sequence continues; Ryan wants to add his own
jokes.punchline: Ryan toasts Kelly's unborn baby — 'Philip Lipton' — joining the Philip name collision, and the 'just four short months' eagerness implies this is also a flex at Pam
jokes.explanation: Extends the Philip name joke to a third party — now three different babies in the same office are all being named Philip. The callback works and adds absurdist escalation to the name joke. Ryan delivering this toast is character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Jim's toast to 'Philip Halpert' — and his elaborate explanation that he promised his grandfather 'as a child, long before tonight' that he would name his son Philip
jokes.setup: Ryan has just toasted Kelly's baby Philip; Jim immediately counters with his own Philip toast
jokes.punchline: 'Long before tonight' — a dig at the competing Philip names, delivered very Jim, implying Ryan and Kelly are copying
jokes.explanation: The competitive Philip toasting is escalating nicely. 'Long before tonight' is a wonderfully passive-aggressive Jim move — he'd never directly accuse Ryan of copying but slides in the jab. Good character voice.

jokes.text: Angela's reaction to Jim's Philip toast: 'She just always has to copy anything I do. It's the Ford Taurus situation all over again.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are toasting their baby Philip after Angela and Ryan toasted theirs
jokes.punchline: Angela thinks SHE was first with the Philip name and Jim/Pam are copying her — mirroring the earlier scene where Angela whispered the name to Pam. 'The Ford Taurus situation' is a mystery callback implying a long history of Pam copying Angela.
jokes.explanation: Angela's righteous indignation about being 'copied' — when she told Pam the name in confidence — is perfect Angela character comedy. 'The Ford Taurus situation all over again' is a great throwaway that implies a rich history of absurd feuds. High character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight's toast: 'I'd like to make a toast to the troops. Here, here. All the troops. Both sides.'
jokes.setup: The toast sequence has been going around the party
jokes.punchline: 'Both sides' — Dwight, in keeping with his weird militarism and contrarianism, toasts all military forces including the enemy
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great two-word punchline. 'Both sides' is perfectly Dwight — his weird military fascination, his inability to pick a side in a conventional way, his contrarian instinct. The self-serious 'Here, here' setup makes 'Both sides' land harder. Extremely quotable, great economy. This is the type of joke that defines a character.

jokes.text: Two separate people attempt to toast Robert California — Oscar then someone else — and Andy intervenes: 'You can't triple-toast somebody. At least not until we hit everyone once.'
jokes.setup: Multiple people keep trying to toast Robert California, apparently to curry favor
jokes.punchline: Andy has to create a 'toast rule' on the spot — you can't triple-toast — revealing that the entire party has devolved into competitive sycophancy
jokes.explanation: The 'triple-toast rule' is a funny piece of invented etiquette. The fact that multiple people keep toasting Robert is funny; Andy having to moderate it is even funnier. 'At least not until we hit everyone once' implies this is an actual etiquette regulation, adding to the absurdity.

jokes.text: Robert California's toast speech: 'You want to toast the man who led you to success, but the boss is irrelevant. Andy and I produce nothing. We do nothing. We sit in our offices and demand, like petulant children.' / 'You know the difference between a crying baby and a manager? One day the baby will grow up.'
jokes.setup: Robert California rises to give a toast after being repeatedly toasted
jokes.punchline: Robert's toast is a devastating self-immolation disguised as generosity — the baby/manager joke is genuinely dark, and he delivers it entirely seriously
jokes.explanation: One of James Spader's best moments as Robert California. The baby/manager joke is dark, original, and perfectly in-character — Robert's brand of uncomfortable charisma applied to a sincere-seeming speech that systematically demolishes management. 'One day the baby will grow up' is an excellent punchline. The delivery — presumably sincere and unironic — makes it funnier and more unsettling. High quotability. Approaches the 8.0 anchor comparably.

jokes.text: Andy tries to continue his toast to Robert immediately after Robert finishes — 'From the moment you entered our building and our hearts, you—' — then gets immediately cut off by Dwight announcing Walter Jr.
jokes.setup: Andy has been trying to toast Robert California the entire party; Robert has just given a brilliant speech
jokes.punchline: Andy's attempt to follow Robert's speech with generic sycophantic filler ('entered our building and our hearts') is immediately trampled by Dwight
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat — 'from the moment you entered our building and our hearts' is painfully generic, which makes it funnier. Being cut off at that moment is appropriate punishment. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Dwight's announcement of Walter Jr.: 'Mr. Walter Banes Bernard, Sir, please report to the stage.'
jokes.setup: Andy wants his brother to perform with him
jokes.punchline: Dwight announces Walter Jr. like a military roll call — 'please report to the stage' — treating the announcement of a party guest like a military summons
jokes.explanation: Maintains the Dwight announcement running gag. 'Please report to the stage' is a funny reframing — it's oddly authoritative for a garden party. Character-consistent.

jokes.text: Andy and his father try to perform 'More Than Words' — the guitar is too high-pitched and they argue about the key while guests watch uncomfortably
jokes.setup: Andy wants a heartwarming father-son duet like his brother had in the viral video
jokes.punchline: The performance immediately collapses into bickering about whether the key is too high — 'It's too high.' / 'It's high but it's not THAT high. Really?' — in front of all their guests
jokes.explanation: The cringe here is earned — we've been set up to understand Andy desperately wants the viral-video father-son moment, and instead he gets a public argument about the guitar key. The bickering in front of an audience is perfectly uncomfortable. Andy's hopeful ambition vs. the cold reality of his actual family relationship.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Is anyone filming this? Seriously. Erin!'
jokes.setup: Andy and his father have finally gotten the song going and it's going reasonably well
jokes.punchline: Andy's priority mid-song is to ensure it's being filmed for viral posterity — revealing that the entire point was documentation, not connection
jokes.explanation: Great character beat — Andy interrupting his own potential viral moment to demand it be filmed is simultaneously sad and funny. The insight is sharp: he's so anxious about replicating the viral video that he can't just live in the moment. 'Seriously. Erin!' escalation works well.

jokes.text: Andy's father to Walter Jr.: 'Get up there and sing, or I will cut your larynx and you'll never be able to sing again.'
jokes.setup: Andy tries to get Walter Jr. to join the duet; Walter Jr. resists
jokes.punchline: Andy's father's casual threat of larynx removal — delivered with the same tone as any parental request — is darkly funny and reveals the family's warped dynamic
jokes.explanation: A darkly funny line that reveals Mr. Bernard as a terrifying parent beneath the patrician surface. Threatening to destroy his son's singing ability if he doesn't sing is an appropriately monstrous non-sequitur. The specificity of 'larynx' makes it funnier than a generic threat. Solidly quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight's Schrute Farms birthday party packages: 'The Pewter package has the least amount of goats. It's not no goats — it's still 10 to 12 goats depending on the availability of the goats.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is pitching Schrute Farms birthday party packages to a potential client
jokes.punchline: The tiered packages are defined by goat quantity — the 'least' package still has 10-12 goats, 'depending on the availability of the goats'
jokes.explanation: The goat packages are excellent Schrute worldbuilding. 'Depending on the availability of the goats' is brilliant — implying goats have scheduling conflicts or other commitments. The fact that the MINIMUM package has 10-12 goats is perfect Dwight logic. High character integration, great specificity. 'Availability of the goats' is very quotable.

jokes.text: Potential client: 'Of course I am not interested in goats. Why would you spend so much time going over the goats with me?'
jokes.setup: Dwight has spent considerable time explaining goat tiers
jokes.punchline: The client's legitimate confusion and frustration — he never asked about goats — deflates Dwight's elaborate goat pitch
jokes.explanation: The straight-man reaction to Dwight's goat pitch. 'Why would you spend so much time going over the goats with me?' is a reasonable question that makes Dwight's pitch funnier in retrospect. Good button.

jokes.text: Dwight's exotic meat upsell: 'I can get you exotic meats. Hippo steaks. Giraffe burgers.'
jokes.setup: Client declines the goat packages
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately pivots to offering illegal/impossible exotic meats as if this is a reasonable alternative party option
jokes.explanation: 'Hippo steaks. Giraffe burgers.' — the specificity of the exotic meat list is excellent. These are not glamorous exotic meats (no truffle or wagyu) — they're just large, unusual animals treated matter-of-factly. Dwight offering to source hippo steaks for a birthday party is beautifully absurd and character-specific.

jokes.text: After the exotic meat pitch, the client's non-committal 'We'll talk' — followed by Dwight's confident talking-head: 'It'll all be goat.'
jokes.setup: Client says 'We'll talk' after the exotic meat pitch
jokes.punchline: Dwight's immediate, total certainty in talking-head: 'It'll all be goat.' — he knows the client has no choice
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous comedy. 'It'll all be goat' is a perfect button — Dwight's complete, unshakeable certainty that despite offering hippo steaks and giraffe burgers, the outcome was always going to be goat. The brevity is the joke. High quotability, excellent economy. This is near-anchor-level for a single line.

jokes.text: Andy's terrible sales call to Cece Halpert (a baby): 'Hello, Cece Halpert. This is Andrew Bernard. I'd very much like to speak with you about your paper supply needs.'
jokes.setup: Andy is apparently making sales calls at the party (or avoiding interaction)
jokes.punchline: He's calling a baby — Jim and Pam's infant daughter — with a formal business pitch, treating her as a legitimate paper prospect
jokes.explanation: Andy cold-calling a baby with a formal paper pitch is beautifully absurd. 'I'd very much like to speak with you about your paper supply needs' in formal sales register addressed to an infant is a great joke. The follow-up 'That wasn't even my worst sales call' makes it even funnier — what happened in the worse calls?

jokes.text: 'That wasn't even my worst sales call.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just pitched paper supplies to a baby
jokes.punchline: His casual self-assessment that this rates below his actual worst calls implies a history of even more catastrophically misplaced sales pitches
jokes.explanation: Perfect button. Five words that open an entire imagined universe of failed Andy sales calls worse than pitching to an infant. The understatement and implied history make this punch far above its weight. Very quotable, excellent economy. The joke does more work than the setup.

jokes.text: Mr. Bernard confronts Andy privately: 'I'm not going to tell you how impressed I am that you're a manager of some rinky-dink branch of a paper company in Scranton, Pennsylvania.'
jokes.setup: Andy confesses he threw the party to make his father proud
jokes.punchline: His father's idea of withholding approval is delivered as a devastating statement of the facts — 'rinky-dink branch of a paper company in Scranton, Pennsylvania' is both objectively accurate and deeply unkind
jokes.explanation: This line walks the line between comedy and genuine cruelty, which is what makes it work. 'Rinky-dink branch of a paper company in Scranton, Pennsylvania' as the definitive description of Dunder Mifflin is darkly funny — it's exactly what the show IS, puncturing its own premise. The cringe is deep because it's also devastating to Andy emotionally.

jokes.text: Darryl's talking head about Andy's family: 'I think if I had parents like that, I'd be trying to convince everyone all the time how great I was, too. Guess we found Andy's Rosebud.'
jokes.setup: Darryl has witnessed the party and Andy's parental dynamic
jokes.punchline: 'Guess we found Andy's Rosebud' — Darryl using the Citizen Kane reference to pinpoint Andy's psychological wound with surprising insight
jokes.explanation: Darryl showing surprising cultural depth with the Citizen Kane reference is itself a good character moment. 'Guess we found Andy's Rosebud' is a smart, economical summation of the episode's theme. Works as both genuine insight and comedy.

jokes.text: Oscar correcting Darryl's Citizen Kane interpretation — 'No, Rosebud didn't explain why he was how he was. It just represented what was important to him as a child that he missed.' / 'Different school of thought. Let's just agree to disagree.' / 'No. You're wrong.'
jokes.setup: Darryl makes a smart cultural reference about Andy
jokes.punchline: Oscar, the self-appointed office intellectual, immediately corrects Darryl's interpretation — the argument about Citizen Kane symbolism in the middle of Andy's emotional crisis is gloriously misplaced — and Oscar's flat 'No. You're wrong' ending Darryl's attempt to agree to disagree
jokes.explanation: Oscar's pedantic film correction is perfect character comedy — he can't let the incorrect Citizen Kane interpretation stand even in an emotionally charged moment. 'No. You're wrong.' as the endpoint of 'let's agree to disagree' is a sharp, character-specific punchline. The incongruity of the debate (while Andy is presumably in tears) heightens it.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'I'm too hot anyway. My body has somehow become acclimated to southern Italy. Isn't that strange? I've never been there.'
jokes.setup: Darryl tries to exit the Citizen Kane argument gracefully
jokes.punchline: He non-sequiturs into claiming his body is thermally calibrated to southern Italy despite never having visited — a completely deranged exit from the conversation
jokes.explanation: A genuinely weird and funny line. 'My body has somehow become acclimated to southern Italy. Isn't that strange? I've never been there.' is a surreal non-sequitur that perfectly captures how people change the subject when losing an argument. The self-questioning 'Isn't that strange?' makes it funnier. High originality — this is a memorable, unexpected joke.

jokes.text: Andy's parents say goodbye: 'It was a nice party. The setting was a little strange. The food... Sandwiches were dry.' / 'Bye, Tuna. Bye, Pam.'
jokes.setup: Andy's parents leave after the party
jokes.punchline: Their perfunctory, slightly critical farewell ('setting a little strange,' 'sandwiches were dry') followed by warmly saying goodbye to Jim ('Tuna') and Pam by name — having more warmth for Andy's coworkers than their own son
jokes.explanation: The cruelest and funniest beat about the Bernards — they dismiss the entire party with mild criticism ('sandwiches were dry') then warmly address Jim and Pam by name/nickname. They know 'Tuna' — Andy has talked about Jim at home — but still can't muster real warmth for Andy. The callback to 'Tuna' makes this sting extra. Well-structured emotional cringe.

jokes.text: Andy's apology to the party: 'Hey, everybody. I'm going to leave and I just wanted to say I'm really sorry.' / 'Cheeseburger or hamburger?'
jokes.setup: Andy delivers a heartfelt apology to his colleagues for the chaotic party
jokes.punchline: Someone is completely absorbed in a different decision and asks 'Cheeseburger or hamburger?' cutting through the emotional moment with mundane indifference
jokes.explanation: The classic sitcom deflation of an emotional moment with complete mundane indifference. 'Cheeseburger or hamburger?' (technically the same thing, which adds an absurdist layer) cutting into Andy's apology is a well-timed reaction beat. The fact that someone is pondering the cheeseburger/hamburger distinction during an emotional speech is perfectly observed.

jokes.text: Oscar calling Andy 'Nard-Dog' — Andy's reaction of genuine, childlike gratitude
jokes.setup: Andy is apologizing and preparing to leave, feeling humiliated
jokes.punchline: Oscar using Andy's nickname 'Nard-Dog' with warmth — a small gesture — and Andy's presumably disproportionate emotional response
jokes.explanation: A warm character beat rather than a pure comedy moment. 'Nard-Dog' lands with gentle humor — the nickname itself is funny, and Oscar using it is an affectionate moment. More emotionally resonant than comedic.

jokes.text: Closing ceremony drumming — 'What are they doing?' / 'Closing ceremonies.' / 'Nice touch.'
jokes.setup: Guests are leaving Schrute Farms after the garden party
jokes.punchline: Mose is performing closing ceremony drumming — a completely unnecessary, probably unsettling formal ritual for a departing garden party — and Jim/Pam respond with mild, amused approval
jokes.explanation: A lovely visual gag — Mose drumming people out of the party like a tribal send-off. Jim and Pam's 'nice touch' understatement is the perfect response. Good use of Mose as an ambient absurdist element. Strong rewatch visual.

jokes.text: Jim keeps returning to the party having 'forgotten' things — returning multiple times — while Dwight announces him with full ceremony each time: 'Mr. James Halpert!' / 'Keys. My keys.' / 'Stop forgetting things.' / 'I didn't forget them. They're right here.' / 'Mr. James Halpert!'
jokes.setup: Jim is leaving the party but keeps coming back
jokes.punchline: Dwight gives him the full 'Mr. James Halpert!' announcement each time — Jim is apparently engineering returns just to trigger the announcement gag, or Dwight can't stop himself
jokes.explanation: A great callback to the guest announcement gag — the running gag completion at the end of the episode. Jim possibly engineering the returns to trigger the announcement is exactly Jim's prankster character. Each 'Mr. James Halpert!' is a mini-callback reward for the audience. Strong structural payoff to the book prank subplot. 'I didn't forget them. They're right here.' while the announcement blares is perfect.

jokes.text: Jim returns one more time ('I think I forgot the—') / Dwight: 'What, you idiot' / Jim asks Dwight who the best salesman in the office is, just to trigger one final 'Mr. James Halpert!'
jokes.setup: Jim keeps returning to trigger the announcement; Dwight is exasperated but can't break from the book's instructions
jokes.punchline: Jim manufactures the final trigger by asking Dwight who the best salesman is — the answer being 'Mr. James Halpert!' — confirming he's been gaming the system the entire time
jokes.explanation: The perfect closing joke. Jim engineering a question whose answer IS the punchline — 'who's the best salesman? Mr. James Halpert!' — is an elegant, structurally sophisticated piece of comedy. It's the complete payoff of three different setups: Jim's book, the announcement gag, and Jim's returns. The question is a trap that forces Dwight to announce Jim, making Dwight complicit in his own manipulation. This is The Office at its structural best — a long-game prank with a perfectly constructed payoff. High rewatch value because you can track Jim's engineering in retrospect.

tmdb_overview: Andy plants the seeds of trying to impress Robert California by throwing a garden party at Schrute Farms. Andy's parents and brother also attend the event, only to make him feel awkward.
